title: Resistance to motion controls spreading
spoken: The diffusion coefficient equals the Boltzmann constant times the absolute temperature, divided by six times pi times the dynamic viscosity times the particle radius.
explanation: Thermal energy competes with viscous drag. Doubling viscosity halves the diffusion coefficient while reducing RMS displacement only by the square root of two. Radius means radius, not diameter.

notes.title: An ideal model
notes.explanation: This equation assumes the dilute spherical tracer and Stokes-drag model; dimensional consistency alone does not establish those assumptions.

notes.title: Diffusion coefficient
notes.explanation: A squared-distance-per-time coefficient. This value comes from the accepted model calculation.

notes.title: Why divide by drag?
notes.explanation: Increasing the denominator reduces diffusivity at fixed thermal energy. This is a model dependence, not a rule that every larger quantity must reduce motion.

notes.title: Thermal energy scale
notes.explanation: Boltzmann constant times absolute temperature supplies energy per particle.

notes.title: A known modern constant
notes.explanation: The SI 2019 constant set supplies this value. It must not be treated as independent historical evidence when trying to infer molecular number.

notes.title: Absolute temperature
notes.explanation: Use kelvin. The laboratory holds viscosity as an independently supplied parameter.

notes.title: The drag coefficient
notes.explanation: Six pi times viscosity times radius is Stokes drag per speed for an isolated sphere in the assumed low-Reynolds regime.

notes.title: Dynamic viscosity
notes.explanation: Viscosity is in the denominator. Doubling it at fixed temperature and radius halves D, not the RMS displacement.

notes.title: Particle radius
notes.explanation: The input is a radius, not a diameter. Confusing them changes the predicted coefficient by a factor of two.

assumptions: Dilute, approximately spherical tracers with no-slip Stokes drag in a homogeneous Newtonian liquid.
Wall corrections, interactions, inertia, and observation noise are not included.
The modern SI 2019 constant set is used; this is not a historical inversion exercise.
